transcript:
This message comes from Schwab.
Investing with Schwab is like a hike with endless trails.
Go solo with self-directed investing,
take stops along the way with trading,
or choose a guide with full service wealth management.
Whatever trails you take,
you can invest your way with Schwab.
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer says he's confident
he'll keep his job as the top Democrat in the Senate next year
when the party retakes a majority,
even as he faces calls from some within the caucus to step aside.
As NPR's Elena Moore reports,
both Independent Senator Bernie Sanders and Democrat Alyssa Slotkin
have come out against Schumer as the next Senate Majority Leader.
Sanders, an independent who caucuses with the Democrats,
told reporters that he believes a major takeaway from the midterms
is that voters want the party to move in a new direction.
I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years.
And I like Chuck, nobody who works harder than Chuck Schumer.
But in my view, the time is now for change.
Senator Alyssa Slotkin echoed that,
calling for colleagues to publicly challenge Schumer
and propose a plan for the first 100 days
that makes good on voter calls to govern differently.
It comes as a handful of incoming Senate Democrats
have also declined to back Schumer for the top job.
Elena Moore, NPR News.
Planet warming pollution from fossil fuels
is expected to drop in 2026, dipping by about 0.4 percent.
The Global Carbon Project,
which tracks global greenhouse gas emissions,
says the drop is due to the Iran war.
NPR's Hadil al-Shaalchi reports.
New research shows that oil pollution saw the biggest drop,
expected to fall roughly 1.9 percent globally,
mainly because the conflict in Iran disrupted fuel supplies,
resulting in decreased demand.
Major emitters like China, the U.S., and the E.U.
all saw modest declines in their fossil fuel emissions.
The new research was presented at the U.N.'s annual climate summit,
known as COP 31,
by an international team of more than 140 climate scientists.
The drop may seem like good news,
but researchers warn it's mostly due to global conflict,
causing supply crunches and not a lasting shift to green energy.
Researchers said that coal use ticked up,
driven by surging power needs in emerging economies like India.
Hadil al-Shaalchi, NPR News, Antalya.
Stocks slumped today after the Labor Department
reported higher-than-expected inflation.
NPR's Scott Horsley reports investors think the Federal Reserve
will respond by raising interest rates next month.
The government's latest cost-to-living index
shows consumer prices rose by four-tenths of one percent in October.
Rising rents accounted for about a third of that increase.
Grocery costs were also up sharply.
The monthly inflation rate was higher than forecasters had expected,
and shows prices continue to climb faster than average wages.
The Federal Reserve was already expected to try to curb inflation
by raising its benchmark interest rate by a quarter percentage point next month.
Fed Governor Chris Waller says a larger half-point rate hike could be warranted.
The prospect of higher short-term borrowing costs
rippled through the bond market yields on 10-year treasuries rose,
which tends to put upward pressure on mortgage rates.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
The S&P 500 lost nearly four-tenths of a percent. The Dow lost three-tenths of a percent.
This is NPR News from Washington.
An appeals court says a federal judge must narrow an order requiring LinkedIn
to divulge journalists' communications to the Trump administration for a leak investigation.
The ruling says the government isn't entitled to a blanket order for LinkedIn
to disclose a broad array of user records belonging to journalists.
"9-1-1 dispatchers have long dealt with fake threats, known as swatting."
NPR's Jaclyn Diaz reports now they're facing hoax calls
using AI-generated voices or background sounds.
"The goal with a swatting call is to draw a big response
from police to a home, business or school. It causes a lot of chaos.
People have been injured and even killed as a result.
AI now makes it very easy to change a voice or background noise
to make a call sound even more realistic and harder to determine what's real and what isn't."
That's a growing concern for 9-1-1 dispatchers.
APCO International, the Association of Public Safety Communication Officials,
and the Public Safety Threat Alliance published results from a survey done in June.
They received more than 760 responses from 9-1-1 dispatchers.
About 14 percent said they were targeted using AI tools.
And APCO believes this will increase as AI tools continue to advance.
Jaclyn Diaz, NPR News.
The family farm where President Jimmy Carter grew peanuts, corn, and sugarcane as a boy
and returned throughout his life will be preserved and open to the public.
Preservation Group the Conservation Fund says the farm should be open to the public
for hunting, fishing, and recreation as soon as next year.
I'm Rylan Barton. This is NPR News from Washington.
This message comes from Angie.
Angie has been helping homeowners find skilled pros to get their home projects done well
for over 30 years.
For everything from minor repairs to major remodels, find reviews, pricing,
and booking at Angie.com or on the Angie app.
